opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the hardest parts of building something like Canvas. With a product like that, quality isn't one number. It's a bundle of behaviors that all have to work together.

The way I think about it, there are a few layers. First, there's the core model capability: can it write well, can it code well, can it reason about what you're asking. That mostly comes from the base model, and when the underlying model improves, everything downstream gets a lift.

But Canvas added a whole new set of behaviors on top of that. The model has to decide *when* to open a canvas at all. If you ask a quick factual question, you don't want a big side panel popping up. If you say "help me draft a blog post," you probably do. Then once you're in the canvas, it has to decide whether to rewrite the whole document or make a targeted edit, and if it's targeted, which section, and how to leave the rest alone. And it has to comment on things in a way that's actually useful rather than nitpicky.

So when we compare versions, we're really looking at each of those behaviors separately. For the trigger decision, you can measure things like precision and recall: is it opening canvas when it should, and staying out of the way when it shouldn't? For editing, you look at whether it respects the user's intent: did it change only what was asked? Did it preserve the voice? For comments, it's more about quality and helpfulness, which is fuzzier.

A lot of that we evaluated with a mix of human judgment and model-based grading. We'd build targeted evals for each behavior, and that let us see regressions that a single aggregate score would hide. You'd sometimes find a new version was better at writing but worse at knowing when to do a targeted edit, or more eager to trigger canvas in situations where it was annoying.

We also leaned a lot on synthetic data to shape those behaviors, using stronger models to generate training examples for specific skills, then checking those against the evals. That's how you can move one behavior without breaking the others, or at least notice when you do.

And then there's the stuff evals don't fully capture, which is how it *feels* to use. You really have to sit with it, use it on your own writing and code, and get a sense of whether it's a good collaborator. Some of the most important signals come from that kind of qualitative, vibes-level testing, and then you try to turn what you notice into something measurable for the next iteration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because Canvas is a really interesting case where the differences in model quality are not obvious from the usual benchmarks. If you just look at MMLU or coding evals, you don't see what matters for Canvas at all.

The way I'd break it down is that Canvas puts the model in a fundamentally different interaction mode. In normal chat, the model is generating a response from scratch each turn. In Canvas, the model is collaborating on a shared artifact. It has to decide when to trigger Canvas in the first place, when to make a targeted edit versus rewrite the whole thing, how to leave comments on a user's writing or code, and how to respect what the user has already written. Those are all distinct behaviors, and we found that stronger base models were not automatically better at them.

So when we were training the models for Canvas, we actually had to build out evaluations for each of those behaviors separately. Triggering was one of the hardest. You don't want it to open a canvas when someone asks a quick factual question, but you do want it to trigger for "write me a blog post" or "help me refactor this function." The earlier versions over-triggered pretty badly, and we got the false positive rate down substantially through synthetic data generation and distillation from larger models. Then for edits, the big quality difference was whether the model rewrote everything when you asked it to change one paragraph. Weaker versions would just regenerate the entire document, which destroys the user's work and the sense that you're co-editing. Better versions learned to make localized changes.

And then the comments feature was its own thing. We had to teach the model to give feedback that's actually useful, like a good editor would, rather than generic praise or fully rewriting the piece in the comment. We had human evaluations where we compared the quality of comments against the zero-shot baseline, and the gains there came almost entirely from post-training rather than from the base model getting bigger.

So my mental model is that model quality for a product like Canvas is really the quality of the behaviors you've shaped, and the raw capability of the underlying model is sort of the ceiling. A more capable model gives you more headroom, but you still have to do the work to turn that into something that feels good to collaborate with. And honestly, the fastest way to understand the differences across versions is to use the product. Benchmarks tell you some of it, but the feeling of whether the model is working with you or over you is something you notice within a few minutes.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the quality of the underlying model from how well it collaborates with you in Canvas. A model can write a good answer, but editing an existing document requires a different kind of judgment: should it rewrite the whole thing, make a small change, or leave a comment? And can it preserve the parts you already like?

So when comparing versions, I’d look at both the quality of the writing or code and how well the model understands the scope of your request. If you ask for a small edit and it changes everything, the result might read well, but the collaboration hasn’t worked. Without specifying which versions we’re comparing, I wouldn’t give a precise ranking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of quality in Canvas as more than the quality of a single answer. It’s also whether the model understands how to work with you on an artifact. Does it know when to create a document, when to make a targeted edit, and when to rewrite something more broadly? Can it preserve the parts you liked while changing the part you asked about?

So two models might both write a good paragraph, but feel very different as collaborators. One might make an unnecessary rewrite, while another makes a precise change that fits the rest of your document. That’s an important dimension of quality for this kind of interface.
